rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage first names earth-level produce whose observation does not require looking up: grain, grapes, and vegetables.
rows.anchor: things which are attached or are born spread out on the earth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Grain is named first because it is the chief nourishment and the other produce supplements it.
rows.anchor: Grain is the most important thing for nourishment; all other things come under it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Grapes exemplify fruit because fruit is next in importance for human nourishment and growth, and grapes are its foremost kind.
rows.anchor: the next most important thing needed for human nourishment and growth is fruit and the king of all fruits is grapes

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qadb usually denotes vegetables eaten raw and ready to eat, but it can also include other vegetables.
rows.anchor: mostly used for vegetables which are eaten raw and are regarded as ready-to-eat

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Olives illustrate tree produce; their oil is nourishing, and Sūrah al-Nūr uses it in a parable about lamps.
rows.anchor: The Qur’ ān mentions its nourishing ability and S ūrah al-Nūr mentions a parable

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dates offered Arabs many benefits: nutritious, profitable to store, and usable for a tasty juice.
rows.anchor: dates were an amalgam of multifarious benefits and blessings

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word for enclosed orchards is followed by a description of their dense, luxuriant growth: branches spread and overlap.
rows.anchor: the purpose is to point to the lushness of the trees

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The general wording for fruit broadens the named examples to all fruits, whether local or foreign, fine or ordinary, and even fruit for birds or animals.
rows.anchor: all fruits are referred to whether they are found in Arabia or in other countries

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The general phrase also extends God's favors to animals, whose needs matter to people even though no specific animal food was named earlier.
rows.anchor: nothing is mentioned for them specially

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abban means vegetation and lush grass; it supplies cattle with food of significance comparable to fruit and vegetables for people.
rows.anchor: means vegetation and lush grass

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ordinary grain husk is also eaten by livestock, but the verse names the widely available fresh green grass that substitutes for human fruits and vegetables.
rows.anchor: Fresh lush green grass is made

rows.speaker: certain narratives
rows.claim: Some narratives say that Abū Bakr or ʿUmar did not know the meaning of abban.
rows.anchor: as is mentioned in certain narratives

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Following Farāhī's research, Islahi rejects the claim that Abū Bakr or ʿUmar did not know abban, since it is an ordinary Arabic word.
rows.anchor: it is a very common Arabic word and that it is not correct that Ab ū Bakr (rta) or ‘Umar (rta) did not know

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The manifest usefulness of these favors implies a human responsibility to God, although that premise is left unstated and supplied by context.
rows.anchor: they do not realize what their responsibilities are

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preceding verses show that the stubborn people know God's rights and their duties; arrogance makes them refuse what conflicts with their desires.
rows.anchor: they reckon that no one can displace or destroy them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṣākhkhah means a deafening blast or roar, like ṭāmmah in Sūrah al-Nāziʿāt; it depicts the terrifying first trumpet blast.
rows.anchor: it will deafen the ears

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The answer to the conditional introduced by idh is omitted as evident from the context; the implication follows the explanation at 79:30–35.
rows.anchor: The answer to the conditional clause

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People who now shut their ears to the Prophet's warning will face a herald whose nearby call deafens them.
rows.anchor: what will they do when the caller deputed by the Almighty will call from such a nearby place

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Even close kin cannot draw attention on that day; a brother will not heed his brother’s pleas.
rows.anchor: Neither a brother will hear the imploring of his brother

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: No one will have the courage to share hardships even with his wife and sons.
rows.anchor: nor will anyone have the courage to share the hardships faced by his wife and sons

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The day's terror will make everyone care only for himself: relatives will not heed pleas or share one another's hardships.
rows.anchor: everyone will be so concerned about his own self on that day that the thought of others will not even cross his mind

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sūrah al-Maʿārij describes the same estrangement and ransom offered by the sinner, but reverses the order of relatives: here distant-to-near, there near-to-distant.
rows.anchor: the sequence of relatives mentioned is from distant to near and in this one it is vice versa

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The dark faces of disbelievers reveal their lost hope and inward condition.
rows.anchor: they would have lost all hope

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The bright faces of Paradise people show the first radiance of joy.
rows.anchor: also denotes joy and happiness.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḍāḥikah denotes joy and happiness, while mustabshir denotes freshness.
rows.anchor: also denotes joy and happiness.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The disbelievers' faces are dark and gloomy because they have lost hope; this is the outcome of their earlier ingratitude, arrogance, and disobedience.
rows.anchor: they would have lost all hope

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse's closing words briefly state the charge against these criminals: in worldly life they were ungrateful, arrogant, and disobedient to God.
rows.anchor: in the previous world they persisted to show ingratitude to God and remained arrogant and disobedient to Him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening upheavals overwhelm people so completely that, apart from the shared catastrophe, they register nothing else, even one another.
rows.anchor: except for the common calamity they would be encountering, their sense will register nothing else

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After resurrection, people are sorted by belief and deeds, the oppressed receive justice, records are exposed, the sky reddens, Hell blazes, Paradise nears, and each sees what he has prepared.
rows.anchor: the circumstances which will arise after the dead are brought back to life are portrayed

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The stars and the night-to-dawn transition testify that the Qur'an is not soothsayer chant but was brought by God's mighty, honored, obeyed, trustworthy angel.
rows.anchor: bear witness that the Qur’ ān is not of the genre of ludicrous chants of the soothsayers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rejecters are answered: the reciter is sane, his meeting with the angel is real, revelation comes involuntarily from God, and the Satan accusation is foolish.
rows.anchor: a messenger of God and a very sensible person

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reminder offers a choice: the Prophet is not to force acceptance, and only people whom God's practice deems worthy gain the courage to choose the right path.
rows.anchor: Neither is it the responsibility of the Prophet (sws) to force it upon them nor is it the practice of God to force them to accept it

none: Text and translation only; no explanatory point.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Takwir means folding or tying something into a bundle, as in wrapping a turban; the verse portrays the sun's extinction.
rows.anchor: to fold something” or “to tie it up in the form of a bundle.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When the sun itself is extinguished, the world it lit will become dark and murky, unlike its ordinary daily concealment from our view.
rows.anchor: the sun will be totally extinguished

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Inkidār means to grow dim or lose shine; with the sun gone, the stars lose their lustre.
rows.anchor: when the sun will cease to exist, all the bulbs and lanterns which rely on its light will automatically lose their lustre

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The deeply rooted, seemingly everlasting mountains will move on Judgment Day and fly like clouds, as other Qur'anic passages explain.
rows.anchor: they will fly about like clouds

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿIshār is the plural of ʿushar and refers to a she-camel ten months pregnant.
rows.anchor: It refers to a ten-month pregnant she-camel

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The neglected pregnant camels illustrate how the upheaval makes people forget others and even their most prized worldly possessions.
rows.anchor: the most favoured and cherished possessions will also have no importance in their eyes

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For the Arab audience, a ten-month pregnant camel was especially treasured because owners guarded it and depended on the anticipated benefits.
rows.anchor: The owners of such camels would take special care of them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qur'an 22:2 conveys the same terror by saying a nursing mother forgets her infant; this passage instead shows even prized property becoming insignificant.
rows.anchor: here the horror of that day is communicated through the insignificance of a prized possession

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wild beasts will gather in refuge, abandoning natural enmities because each fears its own fate.
rows.anchor: forgetting their natural enmities they will gather together in places wherever they expect to find refuge

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In a forest fire or flood, prey and predator may gather on one refuge without recognizing their enemy; Judgment Day will bring this state in its most dreadful form.
rows.anchor: goats, lions and wolves stand alongside one another but none of them will realize that its enemy or prey is right beside it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sajjirat first refers to fueling a stove and came to mean seas in turmoil, overflowing their bounds onto land; 82:3 uses the related word fujjirat.
rows.anchor: It is conventional to refer to seas which get out of control and exceed their boundaries and spread on the land by this word

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The seas are now confined by shores, but the Judgment Day upheaval will make them break beyond their boundaries.
rows.anchor: today these seas are confined in their shores but when the great upheaval of the Day of Judgement takes place, they will burst out of their boundaries

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Soul-pairing means grouping people according to faith and deeds, as detailed in Sūrah al-Wāqiʿah 56:7–44.
rows.anchor: and an explanation of how the Almighty will deal with each of these three

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This world's trial allows good and evil together; after judgment, wrongdoers face Hell while those who pass the test gain eternal success.
rows.anchor: this world is a place of trial and test

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The buried-alive girl exemplifies redress for innocent people oppressed by their own guardians, especially those unable to plead for themselves.
rows.anchor: As an example of this justice, the case

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some Arab fathers killed infant daughters from poverty fears or exaggerated honor; their authority left the girls without rescue.
rows.anchor: overblown honour was also the reason

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question severely rebukes fathers who killed their daughters.
rows.anchor: these callous fathers are severely reprimanded

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opened scrolls are each person's record of deeds, with every deed brought into view, as confirmed by 81:14.
rows.anchor: laying them open means that each and every deed will be brought before them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kashṭ means removing a covering and also stripping an animal's hide; the exposed sky is imagined red like stripped camel meat, as in 55:37.
rows.anchor: means to take off something from the top of a thing

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The following mention of Hell's ignition indicates why the sky becomes red: Hell is set ablaze.
rows.anchor: the next verse of this sūrah mentions that Hell will be set ablaze

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Saʿʿara means to kindle or set ablaze; although Hell is prepared, it flares further when sinners are cast in, since they are its choicest fuel.
rows.anchor: they are the most relished fuel for it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zulfit means bringing something near; Paradise is brought near to the virtuous once people are categorized by deeds.
rows.anchor: to bring something near.” Paradise shall be

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As explained at 50:31, Paradise is already at hand, and bringing it nearer honors its companions by presenting it before them.
rows.anchor: to bring something near.” Paradise shall be

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The final clause completes all the preceding 'whens'; each soul will learn its fate and see what it prepared or failed to do.
rows.anchor: “Knowing” here obviously refers to knowing its fate

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The counterpart sūrah elaborates that every soul learns what it sent forward and left behind, at 82:5.
rows.anchor: what it has sent forward and what it has left behind

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The oath passage refutes the disbelievers' claim that neither the Qur'an is revelation nor Muhammad is God's messenger; they spread this charge to blunt the Prophet's influence.
rows.anchor: the false notion which the disbelievers had invented about the Messenger of God and His Book

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Soothsayers claimed contact with jinn who disclosed the unseen, casting their rhymed utterances as revelation; the Qur'an rejects the idea that the Prophet is their kind.
rows.anchor: like many other soothsayers of their society, he too was a soothsayer

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One basis of Arab soothsaying was astrology: stars were thought to cause events, signal luck, and provide omens through their movement and disappearance.
rows.anchor: they believed that stars per se could effect happenings

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The other basis was the alleged jinn connection: soothsayers staged meditation and presented claimed messages from the unseen.
rows.anchor: they claimed that they had contacts with the jinn from whom they could receive the news of the unknown and unseen world

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qur'anic descriptions of celestial bodies' rising and setting show that they neither control events nor signify luck; their movements are governed by God, as Abraham's reasoning in 6:75–84 illustrates.
rows.anchor: none of them has any authority per se to influence events and happenings

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shooting stars prevent jinn from eavesdropping on the unseen; related passages in Sūrat al-Najm and Sūrat al-Jinn clarify the oath.
rows.anchor: the Almighty has set up a whole system to fend them off

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prefixed lā in these oaths is not denial of the oath; it negates the addressees' claim being refuted by the oath.
rows.anchor: the occurrence of the particle of negation lā before such oaths is not meant to negate these oaths

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khunnas is plural of khānis: something that advances then withdraws, appears then disappears, or becomes evident then hides.
rows.anchor: It refers to something which comes forward and then draws away

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khunnas commonly describes stars, not a particular subset: all kinds, stationary or moving, including planets, fit the description.
rows.anchor: all types of stars whether they are stationery or moving

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because the attributes appear without a conjunction, al-jawārī al-kunnas still describes the same stars; the terms mean traversing and hiding in their destinations.
rows.anchor: all refer to the same noun

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Saʿīd al-Khūrī al-Shartūnī's lexicon says the adjective kunnās applies to all types of stars.
rows.anchor: the famous Arabic lexicon

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The stars' predictable rising, traversing, and setting refute both astrology's claim of independent influence and the alleged celestial eavesdropping sites for jinn; they show subservience to God.
rows.anchor: evidence to their subservience to some higher authority

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The real Lord and protector is God, the wise and powerful authority who can affect events positively or negatively.
rows.anchor: He is the real Lord and Sanctuary for all

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The heavenly bodies are not places where devils eavesdrop; observation posts in the heavens repel them with projectiles.
rows.anchor: these devils are pelted

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The oath is deliberately terse but gives clues: khunnas calls attention to setting as well as rising, which exposes the stars' subjection to a higher being.
rows.anchor: they should also have witnessed their setting which is a very clear evidence of their subservience

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-jawārī al-kunnas subtly evokes stars chasing devils, like lightning or an arrow that reaches its destination and vanishes back into its bow.
rows.anchor: a burst of lightning emerges like an arrow

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The retreating night and breathing dawn form another oath that supports the preceding claim about the Qur'an.
rows.anchor: This is another oath which bears witness from another angle to the premise mentioned

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿAsʿas can mean either grow dark or withdraw and pass away; the author prefers the second sense, supported by the parallel wording at 74:33–34.
rows.anchor: can be interpreted in the light of both these meanings
